H&M Customer Value Segmentation: Full Analysis

MKT566 group project · Data prep, Q1 clustering, Q2 comparison and regressions

Read me first

Business question. H&M’s profit is growing but its sales are flat. Which customers should H&M put its marketing money into, with which products, and through which channel?

Part Question Method Owner Status
Step 0 Clean data, recover quantity data.table Jennie Done
Q1 Who are the most valuable segments? RFM + k-means Jennie, Amelia Done
Q2 steps 1–3 How do segments differ in age, channel, products, price? Per-cluster comparison Howard, Jason Done
Q2 step 4: price Does the price gap hold after age? OLS on log(price per item) Halu Done
Q2 step 4: channel Does the channel gap hold after age? Logit + clustered SEs Trisha Done
Recommendation Which segment, products, channel? Built from all results Angelina To do

How this file runs. By default, knitting rebuilds everything from the raw Kaggle files in data/ and writes every result (tables, charts, data files) to outputs/. The switches in the header can turn the slow steps off once outputs/ exists:

Switch Default Set to false to…
rerun_prep true load the saved cleaned tables instead of rebuilding them
rerun_clustering true load the saved cluster labels instead of rerunning k-means
rerun_channel_check true load the saved channel check instead of re-reading 3.3 GB

Key definitions.

  • Analysis window: 20 Sep 2018 – 29 Feb 2020 (stops before COVID store closures distort the channel mix).
  • Unit / quantity: each raw row is one item, so identical rows (same customer, date, product, channel) are counted as units.
  • Price: scaled by Kaggle, not real currency. Only relative differences are meaningful.
  • Online: sales_channel_id == 2 (checked in Section 4.1).
  • Index: 100 = same as the average customer (all four clusters combined, weighted by units); 120 = 20% more than average.

1 Setup

library(data.table)  # fast reading and grouping of large tables
library(ggplot2)     # charts
# sandwich and lmtest are used in Section 5 (clustered standard errors) via sandwich:: and lmtest::
stopifnot(requireNamespace("sandwich", quietly = TRUE), requireNamespace("lmtest", quietly = TRUE))
options(datatable.showProgress = FALSE)   # keep data.table progress messages out of the report
inp  <- function(f) file.path(params$data_dir, f)   # raw input file
outp <- function(f) file.path(params$out_dir, f)    # output file
dir.create(params$out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(outp("q2_outputs"), showWarnings = FALSE)

# Stop early with a clear message if a needed file is missing
needed <- inp("articles.csv")
if (params$rerun_prep) needed <- c(needed, inp("transactions_train.csv"), inp("customers.csv"))
if (!params$rerun_prep) needed <- c(needed, outp(c("line_items.rds", "baskets.rds", "customers.rds")))
if (!params$rerun_clustering) needed <- c(needed, outp("cluster_labels.rds"))
if (params$rerun_channel_check) needed <- c(needed, inp("transactions_train.csv"))
if (!params$rerun_channel_check) needed <- c(needed, outp("q2_outputs/q2_channel_code_check.csv"))
missing <- needed[!file.exists(needed)]
if (length(missing) > 0)
  stop("Missing file(s): ", paste(unique(missing), collapse = ", "),
       ". See the README: raw data goes in data/, results are written to outputs/.")
# ---- Analysis window -------------------------------------------------------
window_start <- as.IDate("2018-09-20")
window_end   <- as.IDate("2020-02-29")   # also the reference date for recency

# ---- Cluster names, order and colours (used in every Q2 table and chart) ----
cluster_order <- c("Loyal top spenders", "Regulars",
                   "Recent occasional buyers", "Inactive one-time buyers")
cluster_cols  <- c("Loyal top spenders"       = "#1b4f72",
                   "Regulars"                 = "#2e86c1",
                   "Recent occasional buyers" = "#f5b041",
                   "Inactive one-time buyers" = "#a6acaf")

# ---- Product catalog (small, always read) -----------------------------------
# article_id is read as text so leading zeros are kept and it matches the transactions file
articles <- fread(inp("articles.csv"),
                  select = c("article_id", "product_group_name", "product_type_name"),
                  colClasses = c(article_id = "character"))

2 Step 0: Data preparation

Owner: Jennie. Output: line_items.rds, baskets.rds, customers.rds in outputs/.

2.1 Load the raw files

# Transactions: only the five columns we use (31.8M rows)
transactions <- fread(inp("transactions_train.csv"),
                      select = c("t_dat", "customer_id", "article_id", "price", "sales_channel_id"),
                      colClasses = c(article_id = "character"))

# Customers: only id and age (1.37M rows)
customers <- fread(inp("customers.csv"), select = c("customer_id", "age"))

raw_transactions_n <- nrow(transactions)
raw_customers_n    <- nrow(customers)

2.2 Check the raw data

# Row counts and column types for each file
dim(transactions)

## [1] 1371980       2
dim(articles)

##  $ article_id      : chr  "0663713001" "0541518023" "0505221004" "0685687003" ...
##  $ price           : num  0.0508 0.0305 0.0152 0.0169 0.0169 ...
##  $ sales_channel_id: int  2 2 2 2 2 2 2 1 1 2 ...

2.3 Apply the analysis window

# Convert the date column in place (no copy of the 31.8M-row table), then keep the window only
transactions[, t_dat := as.IDate(t_dat, format = "%Y-%m-%d")]
transactions <- transactions[t_dat >= window_start & t_dat <= window_end]

2.4 Clean customers

# Keep only customers who bought something in the window
customers <- customers[customer_id %in% unique(transactions$customer_id)]

# Age stays numeric for analysis; age_label shows "Unknown" when age is missing
customers[, age := as.numeric(age)]
customers[, age_label := fifelse(is.na(age), "Unknown", as.character(age))]

2.5 Recover quantity

# Identical rows (same customer, date, product, channel) = several units of one item.
# units = number of rows in the group; unit_price = the price of one unit
line_items <- transactions[, .(units = .N, unit_price = mean(price)),
                           by = .(customer_id, t_dat, article_id, sales_channel_id)]

# Total units per customer, added to the customers table
customer_units <- line_items[, .(total_units = sum(units)), by = customer_id]
customers[customer_units, total_units := i.total_units, on = "customer_id"]

Check the recovered quantity: units and spend in line_items must match the filtered transactions.

units_total       <- sum(line_items$units)
transactions_rows <- nrow(transactions)
cat("Sum of units in line_items:", units_total, "\n")
## Sum of units in line_items: 22886405
cat("Rows in filtered transactions:", transactions_rows, "\n")
## Rows in filtered transactions: 22886405
cat("Match:", units_total == transactions_rows, "\n")
## Match: TRUE
line_items_value   <- sum(line_items$units * line_items$unit_price)
transactions_value <- sum(transactions$price)
cat("Sum of units * unit_price in line_items:", line_items_value, "\n")
## Sum of units * unit_price in line_items: 644065.3
cat("Sum of price in filtered transactions:", transactions_value, "\n")
## Sum of price in filtered transactions: 644065.3
cat("Match (within rounding):", isTRUE(all.equal(line_items_value, transactions_value)), "\n")
## Match (within rounding): TRUE
# Stop the knit if either check fails
stopifnot(units_total == transactions_rows, isTRUE(all.equal(line_items_value, transactions_value)))

2.6 Build the basket table

# Basket = one customer on one day: number of items and basket value
baskets <- line_items[, .(n_items = sum(units), basket_value = sum(units * unit_price)),
                      by = .(customer_id, t_dat)]

2.7 Cleaning summary and save

cleaning_summary <- data.table(
  step = c("Raw data", "After date filter", "After dropping customers with no purchases in window",
           "Customers with age labeled Unknown", "line_items"),
  transaction_rows = c(raw_transactions_n, nrow(transactions), NA, NA, NA),
  customers        = c(raw_customers_n, NA, nrow(customers), sum(customers$age_label == "Unknown"), NA),
  line_items_rows  = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, nrow(line_items)),
  total_units      = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, sum(line_items$units))
)

line_items <- readRDS(outp("line_items.rds")); setDT(line_items)
baskets    <- readRDS(outp("baskets.rds"));    setDT(baskets)

3 Q1: Who are H&M’s most valuable customer segments?

Owners: Jennie, Amelia. Output: cluster_labels.rds.

3.1 Build RFM (one row per customer)

  • Recency: days from the last purchase to 29 Feb 2020 (lower = more recent)
  • Frequency: number of distinct shopping days
  • Monetary: total spend (units × unit price)
rfm <- line_items[, .(recency   = as.integer(window_end - max(t_dat)),
                      frequency = uniqueN(t_dat),
                      monetary  = sum(units * unit_price)),
                  by = customer_id]
rfm[customers, total_units := i.total_units, on = "customer_id"]

3.2 Transform and standardize

k-means measures distance, so the three variables must be on the same scale. Variables with skewness above 1 are log-transformed first, then all three are standardized (mean 0, standard deviation 1).

skewness <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3

skew <- sapply(rfm[, .(recency, frequency, monetary)], skewness)
print(round(skew, 2))   # original run: recency 0.75, frequency 4.15, monetary 5.90
##   recency frequency  monetary 
##      0.75      4.15      5.90
# log(x + 1) only where skewness > 1, then standardize; originals are kept
for (v in names(skew)) {
  x <- rfm[[v]]
  if (skew[[v]] > 1) x <- log1p(x)
  set(rfm, j = paste0(v, "_z"), value = as.numeric(scale(x)))
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
hist(rfm$recency,   main = "Recency",   xlab = "Days since last purchase", col = "grey80")
hist(rfm$frequency, main = "Frequency", xlab = "Distinct shopping days",   col = "grey80")
hist(rfm$monetary,  main = "Monetary",  xlab = "Total spend (scaled)",     col = "grey80")

3.3 Choose k and cluster

Choose k on a sample. k-means for k = 1 to 10 on 100,000 random customers. The elbow flattens after k = 4, so we use four clusters.

z_cols <- c("recency_z", "frequency_z", "monetary_z")

set.seed(123)
rfm_sample <- rfm[sample(.N, 100000), ..z_cols]

wss <- sapply(1:10, function(k)
  kmeans(rfm_sample, centers = k, nstart = 10, iter.max = 100, algorithm = "MacQueen")$tot.withinss)
plot(1:10, wss, type = "b", xlab = "Number of clusters (k)", ylab = "Total within-cluster SS",
     main = "Elbow plot (100,000-customer sample)")

Assign every customer. k = 4 on the sample, then once on all 1.17M customers, starting from the sample’s centers.

kmeans_sample <- kmeans(rfm_sample, centers = 4, nstart = 10, iter.max = 100, algorithm = "MacQueen")
kmeans_full   <- kmeans(rfm[, ..z_cols], centers = kmeans_sample$centers,
                        iter.max = 100, algorithm = "MacQueen")
rfm[, cluster := kmeans_full$cluster]

# Averages per cluster number: the basis for naming the clusters
cluster_summary_num <- rfm[, .(n_customers = .N, avg_recency = mean(recency),
                               avg_frequency = mean(frequency), avg_monetary = mean(monetary)),
                           by = cluster][order(avg_monetary)]
knitr::kable(cluster_summary_num, digits = 3, caption = "Clusters by k-means number (before naming)")
Clusters by k-means number (before naming)
cluster n_customers avg_recency avg_frequency avg_monetary
3 318152 398.441 1.481 0.136
4 401789 122.642 2.040 0.161
2 326744 74.029 8.384 0.660
1 120387 39.056 21.354 2.663 
# Name each cluster from its averages, NOT from its number: k-means numbers clusters
# arbitrarily, and the numbering differs between computers and R versions.
#   highest average spend                 -> Loyal top spenders
#   highest average recency (longest ago) -> Inactive one-time buyers
#   of the other two, higher spend        -> Regulars; lower -> Recent occasional buyers
avg <- rfm[, .(m = mean(monetary), r = mean(recency)), by = cluster]
top      <- avg[which.max(m), cluster]
inactive <- avg[which.max(r), cluster]
rest     <- avg[!cluster %in% c(top, inactive)][order(-m), cluster]
stopifnot(top != inactive, length(rest) == 2)

cluster_names_map <- setNames(
  c("Loyal top spenders", "Inactive one-time buyers", "Regulars", "Recent occasional buyers"),
  c(top, inactive, rest))
rfm[, cluster_name := cluster_names_map[as.character(cluster)]]

# Keep the team's original numbering (1 = Recent occasional, 2 = Inactive, 3 = Regulars,
# 4 = Loyal top spenders) so the cluster column means the same thing in every saved file
rfm[, cluster := match(cluster_name, c("Recent occasional buyers", "Inactive one-time buyers",
                                       "Regulars", "Loyal top spenders"))]

Stability check. Repeat with a different seed and a new sample. The original run gave the same four segments: sizes differed by fewer than 20 customers out of 1.17 million.

set.seed(456)
rfm_sample2    <- rfm[sample(.N, 100000), ..z_cols]
kmeans_sample2 <- kmeans(rfm_sample2, centers = 4, nstart = 10, iter.max = 100, algorithm = "MacQueen")
kmeans_full2   <- kmeans(rfm[, ..z_cols], centers = kmeans_sample2$centers,
                         iter.max = 100, algorithm = "MacQueen")
rfm[, cluster2 := kmeans_full2$cluster]

# Cluster numbers can differ between runs, so compare the two runs ranked by average spend
rank_summary <- function(col) {
  s <- rfm[, .(n = .N, avg_recency = mean(recency), avg_frequency = mean(frequency),
               avg_monetary = mean(monetary)), by = col]
  setorder(s, avg_monetary)
}
knitr::kable(cbind(rank_summary("cluster"), rank_summary("cluster2")), digits = 4,
             caption = "Original run (left) vs. re-seeded run (right), ranked by average spend")
Original run (left) vs. re-seeded run (right), ranked by average spend
cluster n avg_recency avg_frequency avg_monetary cluster2 n avg_recency avg_frequency avg_monetary

1 401789 122.6424 2.0399 0.1610 2 401771 122.6426 2.0398 0.1610
3 326744 74.0293 8.3842 0.6596 3 326750 74.0325 8.3837 0.6596
4 120387 39.0562 21.3542 2.6631 4 120399 39.0575 21.3536 2.6630 
saveRDS(rfm[, .(customer_id, cluster, cluster_name)], outp("cluster_labels.rds"))

3.4 Load the cluster labels

cluster_labels_dt <- readRDS(outp("cluster_labels.rds")); setDT(cluster_labels_dt)
rfm[cluster_labels_dt, `:=`(cluster = i.cluster, cluster_name = i.cluster_name), on = "customer_id"]
rfm[, cluster_name := factor(cluster_name, levels = cluster_order)]
stopifnot(!anyNA(rfm$cluster_name))   # every customer must have a cluster

3.5 Describe every cluster

total_revenue <- sum(rfm$monetary)

cluster_summary <- rfm[, .(
  customers       = .N,
  share_customers = .N / nrow(rfm),
  avg_recency     = mean(recency),
  avg_frequency   = mean(frequency),
  avg_monetary    = mean(monetary),
  avg_total_units = mean(total_units),
  share_revenue   = sum(monetary) / total_revenue
), by = cluster_name][order(cluster_name)]

cluster_summary_print <- copy(cluster_summary)
cluster_summary_print[, `:=`(share_customers = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * share_customers),
                             share_revenue   = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * share_revenue))]
knitr::kable(cluster_summary_print, digits = 2, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

fwrite(cluster_summary, outp("q2_outputs/q1_cluster_summary.csv"))
share_long <- melt(cluster_summary[, .(cluster_name, `Share of customers` = share_customers,
                                       `Share of revenue` = share_revenue)],
                   id.vars = "cluster_name", variable.name = "measure", value.name = "share")

ggplot(share_long, aes(x = cluster_name, y = share, fill = measure)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 1)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.6)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue", "tomato"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Customer share vs. revenue share by cluster") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "top")

3.6 Q1 answer: which segments matter

  • Loyal top spenders are 10% of customers but 50% of revenue: the most valuable segment and the first priority to retain.
  • Regulars are 28% of customers and 33% of revenue. They already shop about eight times in 17 months, and there are almost three times as many of them as top spenders, so getting them to buy more is the main growth opportunity.
  • Recent occasional and Inactive one-time buyers are 62% of customers but only 17% of revenue.
  • Because the clusters are built from spending and frequency, the revenue gap is partly expected.

4 Q2: How do the segments differ in what and where they buy?

Owners: Howard, Jason (steps 1–3).

4.1 Open question: which sales_channel_id means online?

The dataset does not document the codes. If code 2 is online, its share should jump in spring 2020, when COVID closed the stores. This uses the full file, including months after our window.

if (params$rerun_channel_check) {
  chan <- fread(inp("transactions_train.csv"), select = c("t_dat", "sales_channel_id"))
  chan_month <- chan[, .(share_channel_2 = mean(sales_channel_id == 2)),
                     by = .(month = substr(t_dat, 1, 7))][order(month)]
  rm(chan); invisible(gc())
} else {
  chan_month <- fread(outp("q2_outputs/q2_channel_code_check.csv"), colClasses = c(month = "character"))
}

ggplot(chan_month, aes(x = month, y = share_channel_2, group = 1)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = "2020-03", linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of items in channel 2",
       title = "Channel 2 share by month (dashed line = March 2020, COVID store closures)") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5))

Answer: channel 2 holds 61–74% of items every month until February 2020, then jumps to 85% in March and 100% in April 2020, when only online sales were possible. So 2 = online, 1 = in-store.

4.2 Step 1: Join

Attach cluster and age (by customer_id) and product group and type (by article_id) to every line item.

# := updates line_items in place, so the 20M-row table is not copied
line_items[cluster_labels_dt, cluster_name := i.cluster_name, on = "customer_id"]
line_items[customers, age := i.age, on = "customer_id"]
line_items[articles, `:=`(product_group_name = i.product_group_name,
                          product_type_name  = i.product_type_name), on = "article_id"]
line_items[, online := as.integer(sales_channel_id == 2)]
line_items[, cluster_name := factor(cluster_name, levels = cluster_order)]

# Join check (expected: 0 missing cluster, 0 missing product group, 96,219 missing age)
data.table(line_items      = nrow(line_items),
           missing_cluster = sum(is.na(line_items$cluster_name)),
           missing_product = sum(is.na(line_items$product_group_name)),
           missing_age     = sum(is.na(line_items$age)))
##    line_items missing_cluster missing_product missing_age
##         <int>           <int>           <int>       <int>
## 1:   20543907               0               0       96219

Customer-level table. One row per customer, used for the age and channel-habit charts and for the regressions (customer-level models avoid counting the same customer many times).

cust <- line_items[, .(total_units  = sum(units),
                       total_spend  = sum(units * unit_price),
                       online_units = sum(units * online)),
                   by = .(customer_id, cluster_name, age)]
cust[, `:=`(price_per_item = total_spend / total_units,
            online_share   = online_units / total_units)]

cust_baskets <- baskets[, .(avg_basket_items = mean(n_items), avg_basket_value = mean(basket_value)),
                        by = customer_id]
cust[cust_baskets, `:=`(avg_basket_items = i.avg_basket_items,
                        avg_basket_value = i.avg_basket_value), on = "customer_id"]

cust[, age_band := cut(age, breaks = c(15, 24, 34, 44, 54, 64, 100),
                       labels = c("16-24", "25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64", "65+"))]
cust[, channel_habit := factor(fcase(online_share == 0, "In-store only",
                                     online_share == 1, "Online only",
                                     default = "Both"),
                               levels = c("In-store only", "Both", "Online only"))]
rm(cust_baskets); invisible(gc())

4.3 Step 2: Compare all clusters

4.3.1 Summary table

summary_q2 <- cust[, .(
  customers           = .N,
  median_age          = median(age, na.rm = TRUE),
  share_age_unknown   = mean(is.na(age)),
  online_share_units  = sum(online_units) / sum(total_units),
  share_both_channels = mean(channel_habit == "Both"),
  share_store_only    = mean(channel_habit == "In-store only"),
  price_per_item      = sum(total_spend) / sum(total_units),
  avg_units_per_cust  = mean(total_units),
  avg_basket_items    = mean(avg_basket_items)
), by = cluster_name][order(cluster_name)]

knitr::kable(summary_q2, digits = 3, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

4.3.2 Age (not used to build the clusters)

ggplot(cust[!is.na(age)], aes(x = cluster_name, y = age, fill = cluster_name)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.05) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cluster_cols, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Age", title = "Age by cluster (unknown age excluded)") +
  theme_minimal()

The medians are close (31–36), so the age bands below show the difference more clearly.

age_bands <- cust[!is.na(age_band), .N, by = .(cluster_name, age_band)]
age_bands[, share := N / sum(N), by = cluster_name]

ggplot(age_bands, aes(x = cluster_name, y = share, fill = age_band)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues", name = "Age band") +

  theme_minimal()

4.3.4 Product group (not used to build the clusters)

pg <- line_items[, .(units = sum(units)), by = .(cluster_name, product_group_name)]
pg[, share := units / sum(units), by = cluster_name]

# Overall share of each group (all customers): used to sort rows, drop tiny groups and compute the index.
# Groups under 0.5% of units are dropped: 8 of 17 groups, together only 0.2% of all units.
pg_overall  <- line_items[, .(units = sum(units)), by = product_group_name][, overall_share := units / sum(units)]
keep_groups <- pg_overall[overall_share >= 0.005][order(overall_share), product_group_name]

pg_plot <- pg[product_group_name %in% keep_groups]
pg_plot[, product_group_name := factor(product_group_name, levels = keep_groups)]

ggplot(pg_plot, aes(x = cluster_name, y = product_group_name, fill = share)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#fdfefe", high = "#1b4f72", labels = scales::percent, name = "Share of units") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Each cluster's share of units by product group (columns add to 100%)") +
  theme_minimal()

How to read the index tables below. Each number is an index without units, based on the number of items bought:

index = (share of the cluster’s items in this product) ÷ (share of all customers’ items in this product) × 100

100 = the cluster buys this product in the same proportion as the average customer (all four clusters combined); 151 = 51% more; 84 = 16% less. The index shows the mix of a basket, not the amount: Loyal top spenders buy about 88 items each, so they can have a low hoodie index and still buy more hoodies per person than other clusters.

pg[pg_overall, overall_share := i.overall_share, on = "product_group_name"]
pg[, index := round(100 * share / overall_share)]
pg_index <- dcast(pg[product_group_name %in% keep_groups],
                  product_group_name ~ cluster_name, value.var = "index")
pg_index <- pg_index[order(-match(product_group_name, keep_groups))]

4.3.5 Product-type drill-down

Inside the four largest product groups (82% of all items), which product types each cluster over- or under-buys. Types with less than 0.2% of all units are dropped so tiny types do not produce extreme indexes: 22 of 121 types remain, covering 81% of all items.

pt[pt_overall, overall_share := i.overall_share, on = "product_type_name"]
pt[cl_units,   share := units / i.cl_units,        on = "cluster_name"]   # share of the cluster's units
pt <- pt[overall_share >= 0.002]

4.4 Step 3: Which results are built in?

The clusters were made from recency, frequency and total spend, so:

  • Units per customer and basket size differ largely by construction.
  • Price per item is partly built in (spend = units × price). Present it as “top spenders also trade up a little”, not as a key finding.
  • Age, channel and product mix were not used to form the clusters. These are the real findings and should lead the Q2 slides.

5 Q2 step 4: Do the gaps hold after controlling for age? (Regressions)

Owners: Halu (price), Trisha (channel). Inputs: q2_customer_level.rds, q2_lines_sample10.rds.

Both models enter cluster as a categorical variable with Inactive one-time buyers as the reference group, and control for age. Customers with unknown age (about 1%) are dropped. The results describe differences between segments among customers of the same age; they do not show causes.

cust_r  <- readRDS(outp("q2_customer_level.rds")); setDT(cust_r)
lines_r <- readRDS(outp("q2_lines_sample10.rds")); setDT(lines_r)

ref <- "Inactive one-time buyers"
cust_r[,  cluster_name := relevel(factor(cluster_name, levels = cluster_order), ref = ref)]
lines_r[, cluster_name := relevel(factor(cluster_name, levels = cluster_order), ref = ref)]

cust_m  <- cust_r[!is.na(age)]
lines_m <- lines_r[!is.na(age)]
cat("Customer-level model rows:", format(nrow(cust_m), big.mark = ","),
    "| Line-level model rows:", format(nrow(lines_m), big.mark = ","),
    "from", format(uniqueN(lines_m$customer_id), big.mark = ","), "customers\n")
## Customer-level model rows: 1,152,860 | Line-level model rows: 2,073,508 from 115,345 customers

5.1 Price (Halu): OLS at customer level

log(price_per_item) ~ cluster + age. A coefficient b means the cluster pays about (exp(b) − 1) × 100% more per item than Inactive one-time buyers of the same age.

m_price <- lm(log(price_per_item) ~ cluster_name + age, data = cust_m)
summary(m_price)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = log(price_per_item) ~ cluster_name + age, data = cust_m)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -3.4869 -0.2370 -0.0035  0.2312  2.9283 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                                        Estimate Std. Error   t value Pr(>|t|)
## (Intercept)                          -3.7719912  0.0013206 -2856.330  < 2e-16
## cluster_nameLoyal top spenders        0.1349405  0.0014493    93.108  < 2e-16
## cluster_nameRegulars                  0.0032425  0.0010719     3.025  0.00249
## cluster_nameRecent occasional buyers  0.0065256  0.0010234     6.376 1.81e-10
## age                                   0.0033506  0.0000281   119.251  < 2e-16
##                                         
## (Intercept)                          ***
## cluster_nameLoyal top spenders       ***
## cluster_nameRegulars                 ** 
## cluster_nameRecent occasional buyers ***
## age                                  ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.4265 on 1152855 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.02088,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.02087 
## F-statistic:  6145 on 4 and 1152855 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
price_gap <- data.table(term = names(coef(m_price)),
                        pct_gap = round(100 * (exp(coef(m_price)) - 1), 1))
price_gap <- price_gap[grepl("cluster_name", term)][, term := sub("cluster_name", "", term)]
knitr::kable(price_gap, col.names = c("Segment", "% price per item vs. Inactive one-time buyers"))
Segment % price per item vs. Inactive one-time buyers
Loyal top spenders 14.4
Regulars 0.3
Recent occasional buyers 0.7 
pg_of <- function(s) price_gap[term == s, pct_gap]
fwrite(price_gap, outp("q2_outputs/reg_price_gap.csv"))

Price per item: what we found. Among customers of the same age:

  • Loyal top spenders pay about 14.4% more per item than Inactive one-time buyers.
  • Regulars (+0.3%) and Recent occasional buyers (+0.7%) differ by less than 1%. The differences are statistically significant only because of the very large sample; in practice they are negligible.
  • Each extra year of age goes with about 0.34% higher price per item.
  • Cluster and age together explain only 2.1% of the variation in price per item (R²), so most price differences are between individual customers, not segments.
  • Partly built in: clusters were formed on total spend, so part of the top spenders’ price gap is expected by construction (see Step 3).
  • Consistent with the price index in Section 4.3: the index weights every item (Loyal top spenders 107 vs. Inactive 96), while this model compares the average customer in each segment and controls for age. Both show that Loyal top spenders pay clearly more per item and that the other three segments are roughly level.

5.2 Channel (Trisha): logit at line level with customer-clustered standard errors

online ~ cluster + age on the 10% customer sample, weighted by units. Each customer appears in many rows, so standard errors are clustered by customer (they are 3–4× larger than the default ones). exp(b) is an odds ratio: how many times higher the odds of buying online are than for Inactive one-time buyers of the same age.

m_online <- glm(online ~ cluster_name + age, family = binomial, data = lines_m, weights = units)

# Customer-clustered standard errors
v    <- sandwich::vcovCL(m_online, cluster = ~ customer_id)
test <- lmtest::coeftest(m_online, vcov. = v)

# Odds ratios, 95% confidence intervals and p-values
b  <- coef(m_online)
se <- sqrt(diag(v))
k  <- grepl("^cluster_name", names(b))

results <- data.table(
  Segment = sub("^cluster_name", "", names(b)[k]),
  OR      = exp(b[k]),
  Lower   = exp(b[k] - qnorm(0.975) * se[k]),
  Upper   = exp(b[k] + qnorm(0.975) * se[k]),
  P_value = test[k, 4]
)

# Reference group: odds ratio = 1
results <- rbind(data.table(Segment = ref, OR = 1, Lower = NA_real_, Upper = NA_real_, P_value = NA_real_),
                 results)
knitr::kable(results, digits = 3, caption = "Age-adjusted online purchasing odds (customer-clustered 95% CI)")
Age-adjusted online purchasing odds (customer-clustered 95% CI)
Segment OR Lower Upper P_value
Inactive one-time buyers 1.000 NA NA NA
Loyal top spenders 2.028 1.945 2.114 0
Regulars 0.761 0.735 0.788 0
Recent occasional buyers 1.115 1.073 1.158 0 
fwrite(results, outp("q2_outputs/reg_channel_odds.csv"))
or_of <- function(s) results[Segment == s, OR]
ggplot(results, aes(x = reorder(Segment, OR), y = OR)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#247B91", width = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = Lower, ymax = Upper), width = 0.2, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text(aes(y = ifelse(is.na(Upper), OR, Upper) + 0.08, label = sprintf("%.2f", OR)),
            hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "Online Purchasing Odds by Customer Segment",
       subtitle = "Adjusted for age | Inactive one-time buyers = 1.00",
       x = "Customer Segment", y = "Odds Ratio",
       caption = "95% CIs use customer-clustered standard errors.\nReference OR = 1; no CI estimated.") +
  theme_minimal()

Check at customer level (no repeated rows): online_share ~ cluster + age, coefficients in percentage points of a customer’s units bought online.

m_share <- lm(online_share ~ cluster_name + age, data = cust_m)
s <- coef(m_share)
k_share <- grepl("^cluster_name", names(s))
share_results <- data.table(Segment = sub("^cluster_name", "", names(s)[k_share]),
                            Difference_pp = 100 * s[k_share])
knitr::kable(share_results, digits = 2, caption = "Online share differences vs. Inactive one-time buyers (percentage points)")
Online share differences vs. Inactive one-time buyers (percentage points)
Segment Difference_pp
Loyal top spenders 13.00
Regulars -7.27
Recent occasional buyers 4.52 
fwrite(share_results, outp("q2_outputs/reg_channel_share_pp.csv"))
pp_of <- function(s) share_results[Segment == s, Difference_pp]

Channel: what we found. Among customers of the same age, Loyal top spenders have higher odds of buying online than Inactive one-time buyers (OR = 2.028), Regulars have lower odds (OR = 0.761), and Recent occasional buyers have slightly higher odds (OR = 1.115). All three differences are statistically significant (p < 0.001) with customer-clustered standard errors. Their online shares differ by +13.00, -7.27 and +4.52 percentage points. Both models show that the channel differences from Section 4.3 remain after controlling for age. Channel was not used to build the clusters, so these are genuine differences, but they describe segments and do not explain why they differ.
